questions.latin:
### DISTINCTIO I.

#### Cap. I.
*Omnis doctrina vel de rebus est vel de signis.*

Veteris ac novae Legis continentiam diligenti indagine etiam atque etiam considerantibus nobis, praevia Dei gratia, innotuit, sacrae paginae tractatum circa res vel signa praecipue versari. Ut enim egregius doctor Augustinus ait in libro *de Doctrina christiana*: «Omnis doctrina vel rerum est, vel signorum. Sed res etiam per signa discuntur. Proprie autem hic res appellantur, quae non ad significandum aliquid adhibentur; signa vero, quorum usus est in significando.» Eorum autem aliqua sunt, quorum omnis usus est in significando, non in iustificando, id est, quibus non utimur nisi aliquid significandi gratia, ut aliqua Sacramenta legalia; alia, quae non solum significant, sed conferunt quod intus adiuvet, sicut evangelica Sacramenta. «Ex quo aperte intelligitur, quae hic appellentur signa, res illae videlicet, quae ad significandum aliquid adhibentur. Omne igitur signum etiam res aliqua est. Quod enim nulla res est, ut in eodem Augustinus ait, omnino nihil est; non autem e converso omnis res signum est», quia non adhibetur ad significandum aliquid. Cumque his intenderit theologorum speculatio studiosa atque modesta, divinam Scripturam formam praescriptam in doctrina tenere advertit. De his ergo nobis aditum ad res divinas aliquatenus intelligendas, Deo duce, aperire volentibus disserendum est; et primum de rebus, postea de signis disseremus.

#### Cap. II.
*De rebus quibus fruendum est, vel utendum, et de his quae fruuntur et utuntur.*

«Id ergo in rebus considerandum est», ut in eodem Augustinus ait, «quod res aliae sunt, quibus fruendum est, aliae, quibus utendum est, aliae, quae fruuntur et utuntur. Illae, quibus fruendum est, nos beatos faciunt; istis, quibus utendum est, tendentes ad beatitudinem adiuvamur et quasi adminiculamur, ut ad illas res, quae nos beatos faciunt, pervenire eisque inhaerere possimus. Res vero, quae fruuntur et utuntur, nos sumus, quasi inter utrasque constituti», et Angeli et Sancti. «Frui autem est amore alicui rei inhaerere propter se ipsam; uti vero id quod in usum venerit referre ad obtinendum illud, quo fruendum est; alias abuti est, non uti. Nam usus illicitus abusus vel abusio nominari debet.» «Res igitur, quibus fruendum est, sunt Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus. Eadem tamen Trinitas quaedam summa res est communisque omnibus fruentibus ea, si tamen res dici debet et non rerum omnium causa, si tamen et causa. Non enim facile potest inveniri nomen, quod tantae excellentiae conveniat, nisi quod melius dicitur Trinitas haec unus Deus.» Res autem, quibus utendum est, mundus est et in eo creata. Unde Augustinus in eodem: «Utendum est hoc mundo, non fruendum, ut invisibilia Dei per ea quae facta sunt, intellecta, conspiciantur, id est, ut de temporalibus aeterna capiantur.» Item in eodem: «In omnibus rebus illae tantum sunt, quibus fruendum est, quae aeternae et incommutabiles sunt; ceteris autem utendum est, ut ad illarum perfruitionem perveniatur.» Unde Augustinus in libro decimo *de Trinitate*: «Fruimur cognitis, in quibus ipsis propter se voluntas delectata conquiescit; utimur vero eis quae ad aliud referimus, quo fruendum est.»

#### Cap. III.
*Quid sit frui et uti.*

Notandum vero, quod idem Augustinus in libro decimo *de Trinitate*, aliter quam supra accipiens *uti* et *frui*, sic dicit: «Uti est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis; frui autem est uti cum gaudio non adhuc spei, sed iam rei; ideoque omnis, qui fruitur, utitur; assumit enim aliquid in facultatem voluntatis cum fine delectationis. Non autem omnis, qui utitur, fruitur; si id quod in facultatem voluntatis assumit, non propter ipsum, sed propter aliud appetit.»

Et attende, quod videtur Augustinus dicere, illos frui tantum, qui in re gaudent, non iam in spe; et ita in hac vita non videmur frui, sed tantum uti, ubi gaudemus in spe, cum supra dictum sit, frui amore inhaerere alicui rei propter se, qualiter etiam hic multi adhaerent Deo.

Haec ergo, quae sibi contradicere videntur, sic determinamus dicentes, nos et hic et in futuro frui, sed ibi proprie et perfecte et plene, ubi per speciem videbimus quo fruemur; hic autem, dum in spe ambulamus, fruimur quidem, sed non adeo plene. Unde Augustinus in libro decimo *de Trinitate*: «Fruimur cognitis, in quibus ipsis voluntas propter se delectata conquiescit.» Idem in libro *de Doctrina christiana* ait: «Angeli illo fruentes iam beati sunt, quo et nos frui desideramus; et quantum in hac vita iam fruimur vel per speculum vel in aenigmate, tanto nostram peregrinationem et tolerabilius sustinemus et ardentius finire cupimus.»

Potest etiam dici, quod qui fruitur etiam in hac vita non tantum habet gaudium spei, sed etiam rei, quia iam delectatur in eo quod diligit, et ita iam rem aliquatenus tenet. Constat ergo, quia debemus Deo frui, non uti. «Illo enim», ut ait Augustinus, «frueris, quo efficieris beatus et in quo spem ponis, ut ad id pervenias.» De hoc idem ait in libro *de Doctrina christiana*: «Dicimus ea re nos frui, quam diligimus propter se, et ea re nobis fruendum esse tantum, qua efficimur beati; ceteris vero utendum.» Frequenter tamen dicitur frui cum delectatione uti. Cum enim adest quod diligitur, etiam delectationem secum gerit. Si tamen per eam transieris et ad illud, ubi permanendum est, eam retuleris, uteris ea et abusive, non proprie diceris frui. Si vero inhaeseris atque permanseris, finem in ea ponens laetitiae tuae, tunc vere et proprie frui dicendus es; quod non est faciendum nisi in illa Trinitate, id est, summo et incommutabili bono.

Cum autem homines, qui fruuntur et utuntur aliis rebus, res aliquae sint, quaeritur, «utrum frui se debeant, an uti, an utrumque». Ad quod sic respondet Augustinus in libro *de Doctrina christiana*: «Si propter se homo diligendus est, fruimur eo; si propter aliud, utimur eo: videtur autem mihi propter aliud diligendus. Quod enim propter se diligendum est, in eo constituitur beata vita, cuius etiam spes hoc tempore nos consolatur. In homine autem spes ponenda non est, quia *Maledictus* est *qui hoc facit*. Ergo si liquide advertas, nec seipso quisquam frui debet, quia non se debet diligere propter se, sed propter illud quo fruendum est.» Huic autem contrarium videtur, quod Apostolus ad Philemonem loquens ait: *Ita, frater, ego te fruar in Domino*. Quod ita determinat Augustinus: «Si dixisset tantum *te fruar*, et non addidisset *in Domino*, videretur finem dilectionis ac spem constituisse in eo; sed quia illud addidit, in Domino se finem posuisse eodemque frui significavit.» «Cum enim», ut idem Augustinus ait, «homine in Deo frueris, Deo potius quam homine frueris.»

Sed cum Deus diligat nos, ut frequenter Scriptura dicit, quae eius dilectionem erga nos multum commendat, quaerit Augustinus, quomodo diligit, an ut utens, an ut fruens, et procedit ita: «Si fruitur nobis, eget bono nostro, quod nemo sanus dixerit; ait enim Propheta: *Bonorum meorum non eges*. Omne enim bonum nostrum vel ipse est, vel ab ipso est: non ergo fruitur nobis, sed utitur. Si enim nec fruitur nobis nec utitur, non invenio, quomodo diligat nos.» «Neque tamen sic utitur nobis, ut nos aliis rebus. Nos enim res, quibus utimur, ad id referimus, ut Dei bonitate perfruamur; Deus vero ad suam bonitatem usum nostrum refert: ille enim miseretur nostri propter suam bonitatem, nos autem nobis invicem propter illius bonitatem; ille nostri miseretur, ut se perfruamur, nos vero invicem nostri miseremur, ut illo fruamur. Cum enim nos alicuius miseremur et alicui consulimus, ad eius quidem facimus utilitatem eamque intuemur, sed et nostra fit consequens, cum misericordiam, quam aliis impendimus, non relinquit Deus sine mercede. Haec autem merces summa est, ut ipso perfruamur.» Item: «Quia bonus est, sumus, et inquantum sumus, boni sumus. Porro quia etiam iustus est, non impune mali sumus, et in quantum mali sumus, in tantum etiam minus sumus. Ille igitur usus, quo nobis utitur Deus, non ad eius, sed ad nostram utilitatem refertur, ad eius vero tantummodo bonitatem.»

Hic considerandum est, utrum virtutibus sit utendum, an fruendum. Quibusdam videtur, quod eis sit utendum et non fruendum, et hoc confirmant auctoritate Augustini, qui, ut praetaxatum est, dicit, non esse fruendum nisi Trinitate, id est, summo et incommutabili bono. Item dicunt, ideo non esse fruendum eis, quia propter se amandae non sunt, sed propter aeternam beatitudinem. Illud autem, quo fruendum est, propter se amandum est. Sed quod virtutes propter se amandae non sint, immo propter solam beatitudinem, probant auctoritate Augustini, qui in libro decimo tertio *de Trinitate* contra quosdam ait: «Forte virtutes, quas propter solam beatitudinem amamus, sic persuadere nobis audent, ut ipsam beatitudinem non amemus; quod si faciunt, etiam ipsas utique amare desistimus, quando illam, propter quam solam istas amavimus, non amamus.» Ecce his verbis videtur Augustinus ostendere, quod virtutes non propter se, sed propter solam beatitudinem amandae sint. Quod si ita est, ergo eis fruendum non est. Aliis vero contra videtur, scilicet quod eis fruendum sit, quia propter se petendae et amandae sunt. Et hoc confirmant auctoritate Ambrosii, qui ait super illum locum Epistolae ad Galatas: *Fructus autem spiritus est caritas, gaudium, pax, patientia* etc.: «Haec non nominat *opera*, sed *fructus*, quia propter se petenda sunt.» Si vero propter se petenda sunt, ergo propter se amanda. Nos autem harum quae videtur auctoritatum repugnantiam de medio eximere cupientes, dicimus, quod virtutes propter se petendae et amandae sunt, et tamen propter solam beatitudinem. Propter se quidem amandae sunt, quia delectant sui possessores sincera et sancta delectatione et in eis pariunt gaudium spirituale. Verumtamen non est hic consistendum, sed ultra gradiendum. Non hic haereat dilectionis gressus, neque hic sit dilectionis terminus, sed referatur hoc ad illud summum bonum, cui soli omnino inhaerendum est, quia illud propter se tantum amandum est, et ultra illud nihil quaerendum est; illud est enim supremus finis. Ideo Augustinus dicit, quod eas diligimus propter solam beatitudinem, non quin eas propter se diligamus, sed quia id ipsum, quod eas diligimus, referimus ad illud summum bonum, cui soli inhaerendum est, et in eo permanendum finisque laetitiae ponendus; quare virtutibus non est fruendum. Sed dicet aliquis: Frui est amore inhaerere alicui rei propter se ipsam, ut praedictum est; si ergo virtutes propter se amandae sunt, et eis fruendum est. Ad quod dicimus: in illa descriptione, ubi dicitur *propter se ipsam*, intelligendum est tantummodo, ut scilicet ametur propter se ipsam tantum, ut non referatur ad aliud, sed ibi ponatur finis, ut supra ostendit Augustinus dicens: «Si inhaeseris atque permanseris, finem ponens laetitiae tuae, tunc vere et proprie frui dicendus es. Quod non est faciendum nisi in illa Trinitate, id est, summo et incommutabili bono.» Utendum est ergo virtutibus et per eas fruendum summo bono; ita et de voluntate bona dicimus. Unde Augustinus in libro decimo *de Trinitate* ait: «Voluntas est per quam fruimur»; ita et per virtutes fruimur; non eis, nisi forte aliqua virtus sit Deus, ut caritas, de qua post tractabitur.

*Epilogus.* Omnium igitur, quae dicta sunt, ex quo de rebus specialiter tractavimus, haec summa est: quod aliae sunt, quibus fruendum est, aliae, quibus utendum est, aliae, quae fruuntur et utuntur; et inter eas, quibus utendum est, etiam quaedam sunt, per quas fruimur, ut virtutes et potentiae animi, quae sunt naturalia bona. De quibus omnibus, antequam de signis tractemus, agendum est, ac primum de rebus, quibus fruendum est, scilicet de sancta atque individua Trinitate.

questions.english:
### DISTINCTIO I.

#### Ch. 1.
*All doctrine is either of things or of signs.*

In attentively considering, again and again, the content of the Old and New Law, it has become clear to us, by the preceding grace of God, that the treatment of sacred Scripture turns chiefly upon *things* and *signs*. For, as the distinguished doctor Augustine says in his book *On Christian Doctrine*: "All doctrine is either of things or of signs. But things too are learned through signs. Here, properly, those are called *things* which are not employed to signify anything else; and those are called *signs* whose use is in signifying." Of these signs, some are such that their whole use lies in signifying and not in justifying — that is, we use them only for the sake of signifying something, as is the case with certain legal Sacraments. Others not only signify but also confer that which aids inwardly, as do the Sacraments of the Gospel. "From which it is plainly understood that those things are here called signs which are employed for the sake of signifying something. Every sign, therefore, is also a thing of some sort. For what is no thing, as Augustine himself says in the same place, is altogether nothing. Not, however, conversely is every thing a sign," since not every thing is employed for the sake of signifying something. And since the studious and modest inquiry of theologians has intended these things, it perceives that divine Scripture keeps to a set form in its teaching. Our task, therefore — since we wish, with God's help, to open some way into the understanding of divine things — is to treat these matters; and first we shall treat of things, and afterward of signs.

#### Ch. 2.
*Of things which are to be enjoyed, or to be used, and of those which both enjoy and use.*

"This, therefore, is to be considered among things," as Augustine says in the same book: "some things are to be enjoyed, some are to be used, and some both enjoy and use. Those which are to be enjoyed make us blessed; by those which are to be used we are helped and as it were sustained as we tend toward beatitude, so that we may come to and cleave to the things which make us blessed. The things which both enjoy and use are we ourselves, constituted as it were between the two classes" — we, the angels, and the saints. "To *enjoy* is to cleave in love to some thing for its own sake; to *use* is to refer what has come into use to obtaining that which is to be enjoyed. Otherwise [the act] is *misuse*, not use. For an unlawful use ought to be called *abuse*." "The things, therefore, which are to be enjoyed are the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Yet the same Trinity is one certain supreme Thing common to all who enjoy it — if indeed it ought to be called a thing and not rather the cause of all things, if it is to be called a cause at all. For it is not easy to find a name that suits so great an excellence, except that it is better said that this Trinity is one God." The things to be used are the world and the created things within it. Whence Augustine says, in the same book: "This world is to be used, not enjoyed, that the invisible things of God may be understood and seen through the things that have been made — that is, that from the temporal we may grasp the eternal." Again, in the same: "Of all things, those alone are to be enjoyed which are eternal and unchangeable; the rest are to be used, so that through their use we may come to the full enjoyment of those [eternal] things." Whence Augustine says in Book X *On the Trinity*: "We enjoy the things we know, in which the will, delighted for their own sake, comes to rest; we use, on the other hand, those things that we refer to something else, which is to be enjoyed."

#### Ch. 3.
*What* enjoyment *and* use *are.*

It should be noted, however, that the same Augustine, in Book X *On the Trinity*, taking *use* and *enjoyment* in a different sense than above, speaks thus: "To *use* is to take something into the power of the will; to *enjoy*, on the other hand, is to use with the joy no longer of hope but now of the reality itself. And so everyone who enjoys also uses — for he takes something into the power of the will with the end of delight; but not everyone who uses enjoys, if what he takes into the power of the will he seeks not for its own sake but for something else."

And observe that Augustine seems to say that only those enjoy who rejoice in the reality, not still in hope — and on this reckoning we do not seem to enjoy in this life, but only to use, where we rejoice in hope: since it was said above that *to enjoy* is to cleave in love to some thing for its own sake, in which manner many do cleave even here to God.

These things, therefore, which seem to contradict one another, we reconcile by saying that we enjoy both *here* and *in the future life* — but *there* properly and perfectly and fully, where we shall see through the *species* that which we shall enjoy; *here*, however, while we walk in hope, we enjoy indeed, but not yet so fully. Hence Augustine in Book X *On the Trinity*: "We enjoy the things we know, in which the will itself, delighted for their own sake, comes to rest." The same, in *On Christian Doctrine*: "The angels, enjoying that [God] whom we too desire to enjoy, are already blessed; and the more we already enjoy him in this life — whether through a glass or in a riddle — the more tolerably do we bear our pilgrimage and the more ardently do we long to end it."

It may also be said that one who enjoys even in this life has not merely the joy of hope but also the joy of the reality, because he is already delighted in what he loves, and so already holds the reality in some measure. It is certain, therefore, that we ought to *enjoy* God, not *use* him. "For by that," as Augustine says, "you enjoy by which you are made blessed and in which you place your hope, so as to attain it." Of this the same Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*: "We say that we *enjoy* that thing which we love for its own sake, and that that alone is to be enjoyed by which we are made blessed; the rest is to be used." Frequently, however, *to enjoy* is said to mean *to use with delight*: for when what is loved is present, it brings delight with it. If, however, you pass through that [delight] and refer it to that in which one must remain, you are using it, and to say that you *enjoy* is abusive speech, not proper. But if you cleave and remain, setting the end of your joy in it, then you are truly and properly said to enjoy — which is not to be done except in that Trinity, that is, the highest and unchangeable good.

And since men — who both enjoy and use other things — are themselves things of a sort, the question is asked: "whether they ought to enjoy themselves, or to use themselves, or both." To this Augustine replies in *On Christian Doctrine*: "If a man is to be loved for his own sake, we enjoy him; if for something else, we use him. It seems to me, however, that he is to be loved for something else. For that which is to be loved for its own sake is that in which the blessed life consists, the hope of which consoles us in this time. But hope is not to be placed in man, because *Cursed* is *he who does this*. Therefore, if you clearly mark it, no one ought to enjoy even himself, because one ought not to love oneself for one's own sake, but for the sake of that which is to be enjoyed." Yet against this seems to stand what the Apostle says to Philemon: *Thus, brother, may I enjoy you in the Lord*. Augustine resolves it thus: "If he had said only *may I enjoy you*, and not added *in the Lord*, he would have seemed to place the end and hope of his love in him; but because he added the former, he signified that he placed his end *in the Lord* and that he enjoyed him." "For," as the same Augustine says, "when you enjoy a man in God, you enjoy God rather than man."

But since God loves us — as Scripture frequently says, commending his love for us greatly — Augustine asks in what way he loves us: whether as using or as enjoying. He proceeds thus: "If he enjoys us, he needs our good, which no sane person would say. For the Prophet says: *You have no need of my goods.* Every good of ours is either himself or from him; therefore he does not enjoy us, but uses us. And if he neither enjoys us nor uses us, I do not see how he loves us." "Yet he does not use us as we use other things. For we refer the things we use to this end — that we may fully enjoy God's goodness. But God refers our use [of us] to his own goodness: for he has mercy on us for the sake of his own goodness, while we have mercy on each other for the sake of his goodness. He has mercy on us that we may fully enjoy him; we have mercy on each other that we may enjoy him. For when we have mercy on someone and help him, we do so for his benefit and with an eye to it, but our own benefit follows, since God does not leave without reward the mercy we show to others. This reward is supreme: that we enjoy Him himself." Again: "Because he is good, we are; and insofar as we are, we are good. Further, because he is also just, we are not *with impunity* evil; and insofar as we are evil, so much the less we even are. That use, therefore, by which God uses us is referred not to his utility but to ours — and only to his goodness."

Here it must be considered whether the virtues are to be used or enjoyed. Some think they are to be used and not enjoyed, and they confirm this by the authority of Augustine, who — as was noted above — says that nothing is to be enjoyed except the Trinity, that is, the highest and unchangeable good. They say further that the virtues are not to be enjoyed, because they are not to be loved for their own sake but for the sake of eternal beatitude: for that which is to be enjoyed is to be loved for its own sake. And they prove by the authority of Augustine that the virtues are not to be loved for their own sake but only on account of beatitude. For in Book XIII *On the Trinity*, against certain persons, he says: "Perhaps the virtues, which we love only for beatitude's sake, dare to persuade us that we do not love beatitude itself. If they do this, we certainly cease to love them too, once we cease to love that for the sake of which alone we loved them." Look: by these words Augustine seems to show that the virtues are to be loved not for their own sake but only for the sake of beatitude. And if this is so, then they are not to be enjoyed. Others, however, think the contrary: namely, that the virtues are to be enjoyed, because they are to be sought and loved for their own sake. And they confirm this by the authority of Ambrose, who says, on the verse of the Epistle to the Galatians, *But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, etc.*: "He does not here name them *works* but *fruits*, because they are to be sought for their own sake." And if they are to be sought for their own sake, then they are to be loved for their own sake. We, desiring to remove this apparent conflict of authorities, say that the virtues are to be sought and loved both for their own sake *and* for the sake of beatitude alone. They are to be loved for their own sake because they delight their possessors with a sincere and holy delight and give birth in them to spiritual joy. Yet one must not stop here but go further. Here let the step of love not pause, nor here let the term of love be set; but let it be referred to that highest good, to which alone one must absolutely cleave — for that alone is to be loved for its own sake, and beyond it nothing is to be sought: for that is the supreme end. So Augustine says that we love the virtues "for beatitude's sake alone" — not as though we do not love them for their own sake, but because the very fact that we love them we refer to that highest good, to which alone one must cleave, in which one must remain, and in which the end of one's gladness must be placed. Therefore the virtues are not to be enjoyed. But someone may say: *To enjoy* is to cleave in love to some thing *for its own sake*, as was said above; if, therefore, the virtues are to be loved for their own sake, then they are to be enjoyed. To this we say: in that description, where one reads *for its own sake*, one must understand *only insofar as one loves it for its own sake alone*, so that it not be referred to anything else but the end be set in it — as Augustine shows above when he says: "If you cleave and remain, setting the end of your joy in it, then you are truly and properly said to enjoy; which is not to be done except in that Trinity, that is, the highest and unchangeable good." Therefore the virtues are to be *used*, and through them we are to *enjoy* the highest good. The same we say of the good will. Whence Augustine in Book X *On the Trinity*: "The will is that by which we enjoy"; and so we enjoy through the virtues, but not the virtues themselves — unless perhaps some virtue is God, as is charity, of which we shall treat later.

*Epilogue.* The sum, therefore, of what has been said — now that we have treated of things specifically — is this: some things are to be enjoyed, some are to be used, and some both enjoy and use. Among those which are to be used, there are also some *through which we enjoy* — namely, the virtues and the powers of the mind, which are natural goods. Concerning all of these, before we treat of signs, something must be said — and first of the things which are to be enjoyed, namely, the holy and undivided Trinity.

---
questions.notes:
- **Chunk scope.** This chunk contains the three chapters of Distinction 1 from Peter Lombard's *Sentences* (Bk. I, d. 1, cc. 1–3), as reprinted at the head of Bonaventure's commentary in the Quaracchi edition (pp. 26–28). The three chapters cover: (1) Lombard's general statement that all doctrine is either of things or of signs; (2) the Augustinian distinction among things to be enjoyed, things to be used, and those that both enjoy and use; and (3) the reconciliation of Augustine's two senses of *uti / frui* (the one from *De doctrina christiana*, the other from *De Trinitate* X), followed by the Epilogue that frames the rest of Distinction 1.

- **Nature of the chunk.** This is *Lombard's text*, not Bonaventure's commentary. Bonaventure's own treatment of Dist. 1 appears in the companion chunks `bon-sent-I-d1-a1-q1` through `bon-sent-I-d1-a3-q2` and the `bon-sent-I-d1-dubia` file. The Littera Magistri is included at the head of every distinction so that readers can see the text Bonaventure is commenting on.

- **Sources cited by Lombard.** Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* I.2.2, 3.3, 4.4, 22.20–21, 31–33, 34, 37; Augustine, *On the Trinity* X.10.13, 11.17, 13.22, and XIII.8.11; Ambrose on Galatians 5:22. The debate on the virtues in Ch. 3 reproduces Augustine's *De Trinitate* XIII.8.11 verbatim.

- **Key terms** (per project glossary, shared with the accompanying Bonaventure chunks): *frui / uti / fruibile / utibile* → enjoy / use / enjoyable / usable; *abuti* → misuse / abuse; *cleave* is used consistently for *inhaerere*; *beatus* → blessed; *per speciem* → through the species (i.e. in direct vision, as opposed to in hope).

- **Transcription status.** Lightly cleaned from the raw OCR (`raw/bonaventure_vol1_raw.txt`, lines 12780–13213). Major typos fixed; word-level verification against the PDF is still pending. The English translation is a first-pass rendering of Lombard's text and is intended to give readers unfamiliar with Latin access to the text that Bonaventure is commenting on throughout the remaining chunks of Dist. 1.

questions.title: Dist. 1, Art. 1, Q. 1
questions.titleLa: Utrum uti sit actus voluntatis, an rationis, vel omnis potentiae
questions.titleEn: Whether use is an act of the will, of reason, or of every faculty
questions.latin:
<!-- page 30 -->

**ARTICULUS I.** *Quid sit* uti *et de* utibili.

**QUAESTIO I.** *Utrum* uti *sit actus voluntatis, an rationis, vel omnis potentiae.*

Circa primum[^1] *de uti*, quid sit per essentiam, utrum sit actus voluntatis, an rationis, sic proceditur. Quod sit actus voluntatis ostenditur sic.

1. Ab actu utendi denominatur unusquisque bonus[^2]; sed nullus dicitur bonus nisi ab actu voluntatis: ergo actus utendi pertinet ad voluntatem.

2. Item, Augustinus decimo *de Trinitate*[^3]: «Uti est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis»; ergo *uti* est actus voluntatis.

3. Item, hoc videtur per divisionem ipsius *uti* contra alia, quia decimo *de Trinitate*[^4] dividit Augustinus haec tria, *ingenium*, *doctrinam* et *usum*, et dicit, quod *ingenium* respicit, quid homo possit, *doctrina*, quid homo sciat, *usus*, quid[^5] velit; ergo *usus* est actus voluntatis.

4. Item, «Opposita nata sunt fieri circa idem[^6]»; sed *uti* et *abuti* sunt opposita, ergo cum *abuti* sit solius voluntatis, quia eius solius est peccare: ergo et *uti* similiter erit actus solius voluntatis.

**Contra:**

1. *Usus* sive *assuefactio* est via in habitum acquirendum[^7]; sed omnis potentia nata est acquirere habitum: ergo *uti* videtur esse omnis potentiae.

2. Item, omnis potentia mediante operatione sua ordinatur in finem[^8]; sed eo dicitur aliquid *utibile* sive *uti*, quo in finem est ordinabile; sed ordinari in finem mediante propria operatione est omnis potentiae: ergo et *uti* similiter.

3. Item, sicut Augustinus dicit et habetur in littera[^9], *uti* est id quod in usum venerit referre etc. Sed eius est referre, cuius est conferre; sed conferre est solius rationis, ergo et referre: ergo et *uti* a definitione.

4. Item, *ars* utitur suis instrumentis[^10]; sed *ars* est in potentia rationali sive cognitiva, cum sit scientia: ergo cum habitus et actus sint eiusdem potentiae, si *ars* est in potentia rationali, et *usus* similiter erit in eadem.

> **Conclusio.**
>
> *Uti quinque modis potest intelligi: si sumitur communissime et communiter, est actus omnis potentiae; si sumitur proprie, magis proprie et propriissime, est actus voluntatis.*

**Respondeo[^11]:** Dicendum, quod *uti* quinque modis accipitur, et secundum hoc diversificatur secundum rem et secundum definitionem.

Accipitur enim *usus* sive *uti* *communissime*, secundum quod dividitur contra otium vel otiositatem, pro naturali operatione debita cuilibet rei, sive

<!-- page 31 -->

ad quam unaquaeque res ordinatur, et secundum hoc dicit Philosophus[^12]: «Cuius usus bonus etc.».

Secundo modo dicitur *communiter*; et sic *usus* dividitur contra dissuetudinem. Et hoc modo definitur a Victorino[^13]: «Usus est actus frequenter elicitus a potentia», et hoc modo potest dici, quod est actus omnis potentiae nec addit super actum nisi frequentiam.

Tertio modo accipitur *uti* *proprie*; et sic dividitur contra habitus memoriae et intelligentiae, scilicet[^14] contra *ingenium* et *doctrinam*. Et sic definitur ab Augustino decimo *de Trinitate*: «Uti est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis», et sic dicit actum voluntatis proprie.

Quarto modo accipitur *magis proprie*; et sic dividitur contra actum quietativum, scilicet contra *frui*. Et sic definitur ab Augustino[^15]: «Uti est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis propter aliud», et sic est actus voluntatis ut ad aliud relatae.

Quinto accipitur *propriissime*; et sic dividitur contra actum inordinatum, scilicet contra *abuti*. Et sic definitur ab Augustino *de Doctrina christiana*[^16]: «Uti est id quod in usum venerit referre ad id, quo fruendum est», et sic *uti* dicit actum voluntatis relatum et ordinatum in finem.

Ratio ergo diversarum notificationum est multiplex acceptio eius quod est *uti*; et ratio multiplicis acceptionis est oppositio eius ad diversa.

Si ergo quaeratur, cuius potentiae est[^17] actus: dicendum, quod, communissime et communiter loquendo, est actus omnis potentiae; et sic non loquitur Augustinus; *proprie* vero, *magis proprie* et *propriissime* actus est ipsius voluntatis.

**Ad 1.** Et sic patet primo obiectum in contrarium, scilicet quod[^18] sit omnis potentiae.

**Ad 2.** Quod obiicitur secundo, quod omnis potentia refertur in finem per actum suum: dicendum, quod illa potentia dicitur *uti* suo actu, quae est domina sui actus; et talis potentiae est referre suum actum, non tantum referri. Et quoniam sola voluntas est domina sui actus et sola est se ipsam movens, ideo ipsa sola est, cuius est active *uti*. Aliis autem potentiis contingit *uti* materialiter et passive, quia habent referri, et non referre. Et hinc est, quod ab Augustino dicitur[^19]: «Uti est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis»; *facultas* enim dicitur eius dominium, quo faciliter potest in actum suum tanquam illius princeps.

**Ad 3.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod rationis est referre: dicendum, quod dupliciter est referre, scilicet per *collationem* et *illationem*, sicut praemissae referuntur ad conclusionem; et hoc est rationis, et hoc non est *uti*. Et est referre per[^20] *inclinationem* et *ordinationem* ad aliud; et hoc est proprie voluntatis, quia potest aliquid assumere quiescendo ibi, vel aliud intendendo; et hoc est referre[^21], per quod definitur *uti* etc.

**Ad 4.** Ad illud quod obiicitur de arte, dicendum, quod *ars* dicit quod est *operationis*, et quod est *speculationis*. Secundum quod dicit[^22] quod est *speculationis*, non habet *uti*, et sic est rationis; secundum vero quod dicit quod est *operationis*, sic extenditur ad voluntatem et eam regulat in utendo.

<!-- page 30 -->

**Article I.** *What* use *is, and concerning the* usable.

**Question I.** *Whether* use *is an act of the will, of reason, or of every faculty.*

Concerning the first[^1] — *concerning use*, what it is in essence, whether it is an act of the will or of reason — we proceed thus. That it is an act of the will is shown as follows.

1. From the act of using each one is called good[^2]; but no one is called good except from an act of the will: therefore the act of using pertains to the will.

2. Again, Augustine in Book X[^3] *On the Trinity*: "To use is to take something into the power of the will"; therefore *use* is an act of the will.

3. Again, this seems [to follow] from the division of *use* itself against other things, since in Book X *On the Trinity*[^4] Augustine divides these three — *ingenuity*, *teaching*, and *use* — and says that *ingenuity* considers what man is able [to do], *teaching* what man knows, *use* what[^5] he wills; therefore *use* is an act of the will.

4. Again, "Opposites are by nature concerned with the same thing[^6]"; but *use* and *misuse* are opposites; therefore since *misuse* belongs to the will alone, because to sin belongs to it alone: therefore *use* likewise will be the act of the will alone.

**On the contrary:**

1. *Use* or *habituation* is the way to acquiring a habit[^7]; but every faculty is by nature able to acquire a habit: therefore *use* seems to belong to every faculty.

2. Again, every faculty is ordered to its end through its own operation[^8]; but a thing is called *usable* or said to be *used* by reason of that whereby it is orderable to an end; but to be ordered to an end through one's own operation belongs to every faculty: therefore *use* likewise [belongs to every faculty].

3. Again, as Augustine says, and as it stands in the *littera*[^9], *to use* is to refer what has come into use, etc. But to refer is the office of him whose office is to confer; but conferring belongs only to reason — therefore [the office of] referring also: therefore *use* too [belongs to reason], by [its very] definition.

4. Again, *art* uses its instruments[^10]; but *art* is in a rational or cognitive power, since it is a science: therefore, since habit and act belong to the same faculty, if *art* is in a rational power, *use* likewise will be in the same.

> **Conclusion.**
>
> *"Use" can be understood in five ways: if taken most commonly and commonly, it is an act of every faculty; if taken properly, more properly, and most properly, it is an act of the will.*

**I respond[^11]:** It must be said that *use* is taken in five ways, and accordingly its meaning and its definition are differentiated.

For *use* or *to use* is taken *most commonly*, insofar as it is divided against idleness or inactivity — [namely] for the natural operation owed to each thing, or that

<!-- page 31 -->

to which each thing is ordered; and in this sense the Philosopher says[^12]: "That whose use is good, etc."

In the second way it is said *commonly*; and in this way *use* is divided against disuse. And in this way it is defined by Victorinus[^13]: "Use is an act frequently elicited from a power"; and in this way it can be said that it is the act of every faculty and adds nothing to the act except frequency.

In the third way *use* is taken *properly*; and in this way it is divided against the habits of memory and understanding — namely[^14], against *ingenuity* and *teaching*. And in this way it is defined by Augustine in Book X *On the Trinity*: "To use is to take something into the power of the will"; and in this way it expresses an act of the will properly.

In the fourth way it is taken *more properly*; and in this way it is divided against the quietative act — namely, against *enjoyment*. And in this way it is defined by Augustine[^15]: "To use is to take something into the power of the will for the sake of something else"; and in this way it is the act of the will as referred to something else.

In the fifth way it is taken *most properly*; and in this way it is divided against the disordered act — namely, against *misuse*. And in this way it is defined by Augustine *On Christian Doctrine*[^16]: "To use is to refer what has come into use to that which is to be enjoyed"; and in this way *use* expresses an act of the will referred and ordered to its end.

The ground, therefore, of the various definitions is the manifold acceptance of what *use* is; and the ground of the manifold acceptance is its opposition to different things.

If, then, it be asked of which faculty it is the act[^17]: it must be said that, speaking most commonly and commonly, it is the act of every faculty (and Augustine does not speak in this sense); but *properly*, *more properly*, and *most properly*, the act is of the will itself.

**Reply 1.** And so the first objection on the contrary side is clear — namely, that[^18] it is of every faculty.

**Reply 2.** As to the second objection, that every faculty is referred to its end through its own act: it must be said that that faculty is said to *use* its own act which is mistress of its own act; and it belongs to such a faculty to refer its own act, not merely to be referred. And since the will alone is mistress of its own act, and alone is self-moving, therefore it alone is the faculty whose role is actively to *use*. To the other faculties it falls to be *used* materially and passively, since they have to be referred and not [themselves] to refer. And from this it is that Augustine says[^19]: "To use is to take something into the power of the will"; for *power* (*facultas*) is said to be the will's mastery, by which it can readily pass into its own act as its sovereign.

**Reply 3.** As to the objection that to refer belongs to reason: it must be said that referring is twofold — namely, by *comparison* and *inference*, as premises are referred to a conclusion; and this belongs to reason, and this is not *use*. And there is referring by[^20] *inclination* and *ordering* toward something else; and this properly belongs to the will, since it can take something up either by resting in it or by intending something further; and this is the referring[^21] by which *use* is defined, etc.

**Reply 4.** As to the objection concerning art: it must be said that *art* covers what pertains to *operation* and what pertains to *speculation*. Insofar as it covers[^22] what is *speculative*, it does not involve *use*, and so belongs to reason; but insofar as it covers what is *operative*, it extends to the will and regulates it in *using*.

apparatus.la: *Consentientibus mss. et ed. 1, restituimus verba* Circa primum *et mox mutavimus* aut *in* an, *quod et grammatice melius est.*
apparatus.en: With the agreement of the manuscripts and ed. 1, we have restored the words *Circa primum* and immediately afterward changed *aut* to *an*, which is also grammatically better.

apparatus.la: *Forsitan respicitur illud Arist. II. Ethic. c. 3. in fine: Qui enim bene his (voluptatibus et doloribus) utetur, bonus; qui male, erit malus.*
apparatus.en: Perhaps reference is made to Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* II, ch. 3, at the end: "He who uses these (pleasures and pains) well will be good; he who [uses them] badly will be bad."

apparatus.la: *Cap. 11. n. 17; vide supra in lit. Magistri, c. 3. in initio.*
apparatus.en: Ch. 11, n. 17; see above in the *littera* of the Master, ch. 3, at the beginning.

apparatus.la: *Ibidem, paulo ante; et XI. de Civ. Dei, c. 25.*
apparatus.en: Same place, a little earlier; and *On the City of God* XI, ch. 25.

apparatus.la: *Cod. X hic iterum addit* homo.
apparatus.en: Cod. X here adds again *homo*.

apparatus.la: *Arist., De Praedicam. c. de Oppositis circa finem: Palam vero est, quod circa idem aut specie aut genere nata sunt fieri contraria.*
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Categories*, ch. *On Opposites*, near the end: "It is plain, however, that contraries are by nature concerned with the same thing, either in species or in genus."

apparatus.la: *Idem B. Albert., S. I. tr. 2. q. 8. m. 1. his verbis exprimit:* Secundo dicitur uti rei exercitium ad inducendum habitum, secundum quod dicit Victorinus in Rhetoricis suis (seu Comment. in Rhetor. Ciceronis, l. c. 25. et n. c. 39.), quod natura habilem facit, ars potentem, usus facilem. *— Vide et Aristot., II. Ethic. c. 1.*
apparatus.en: The same Bl. Albert in *Summa* I, tr. 2, q. 8, m. 1 expresses it in these words: "*Use* is, secondly, said [to be] the exercise of the thing for inducing the habit, according to what Victorinus says in his *Rhetorica* (or rather his Commentary on Cicero's *Rhetorica*, l. c. 25 and n. c. 39): nature makes [one] capable, art [makes one] competent, use [makes one] proficient." — See also Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* II, ch. 1.

apparatus.la: *Vide Aristot., IX. Metaph. text. 16. (Ed. Paris. VIII. c. 8.). — Mox codd. CFGHKLORSU cc et ed. 1* utile *pro* utibile; *cod. Z* utile sive utibile *quo etc.*
apparatus.en: See Aristotle, *Metaphysics* IX, text 16 (Paris ed. VIII, ch. 8). — In the next phrase, codices CFGHKLORSU and cc, and ed. 1, read *utile* in place of *utibile*; cod. Z reads *utile sive utibile quo* etc.

apparatus.la: *Hic, c. 2. — Faventibus mss. et edd. 1, 2, 3, 6, pro* infra *substituimus* in littera. *In conclusione huius argumenti Vat.* ergo referre et per consequens uti; *praeferimus tamen lectionem fere omnium mss. et ed. 1 tanquam distinctiorem.*
apparatus.en: Here [in d. 1], ch. 2. — With the support of the manuscripts and editions 1, 2, 3, and 6, we have substituted *in littera* for *infra*. At the end of this argument the Vatican edition has *ergo referre et per consequens uti*; we nevertheless prefer the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and ed. 1 as more clearly worded.

apparatus.la: *Arist., I. de Anima, text. 53. (c. 3.). — Circa finem argumenti mendum Vat. ponentis* sic *pro* si *castigatur ex mss. et ed. 1. — Mox Vat. post* usus *addit* sive uti; *quod deest in antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1.*
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *On the Soul* I, text 53 (ch. 3). — Near the end of the argument, an error of the Vatican edition (which has *sic* in place of *si*) is corrected from the manuscripts and ed. 1. — Next, after *usus* the Vatican adds *sive uti*, which is missing from the older manuscripts and ed. 1.

apparatus.la: *Plures codd. ut A I T etc.* Solutio *pro* Respondeo.
apparatus.en: Several codices (such as A, I, T, etc.) have *Solutio* in place of *Respondeo*.

apparatus.la: *Sententia:* Cuius usus bonus est, ipsum quoque bonum est, *verbotenus legitur apud Boethium, de Differentiis topicis, libr. II. circa medium, in quo libro auctor proponit locorum topicorum divisiones, quae ex una parte, duce Aristotele, a Themistio, et ex altera parte a Cicerone exhibentur, earumque differentias indicat.*
apparatus.en: The maxim *"that whose use is good is itself also good"* stands word-for-word in Boethius, *On the Different Kinds of Topics*, Bk. II, near the middle, in which book the author sets out the divisions of the topics drawn up on the one side by Themistius (following Aristotle) and on the other side by Cicero, and notes the differences between them.

apparatus.la: *Fabius Marius (Laurentius) Victorinus, Rhetor († inter 370–382), qui praeter opuscula theologica contra Arianos varios confecit libros philosophicos et rhetoricos; sic transtulit Porphyrii librum de Praedicabilibus in linguam latinam (cfr. Boeth., Dialogus I. in Porphyrium) scripsitque commentarium in Rhetorica et Topica Ciceronis (cfr. Boeth. Comment. in Topica Ciceronis; et ed. Operum Ciceronis per Orelli, ubi Victorini Comment. in Rhetor. invenitur). Licet definitio* usus, *de qua hic agitur, explicite non inveniatur in praenotatis Victorini operibus, colligi tamen posse videtur ex supra (argum. 1. ad opp.) allatis eius verbis una cum hac exercitationis definitione, quam in Comment. super I. Rhetor. Ciceronis, c. 2. proponit:* Exercitatio est suscepti operis continuatio. *Cfr. et ibid. c. 25., ubi de definitione* habitus *agitur, in qua ponitur* usus *sive* exercitatio.
apparatus.en: Fabius Marius (Laurentius) Victorinus, the Rhetor (died between 370 and 382), who, besides his theological tracts against the Arians, composed various philosophical and rhetorical works; thus he translated Porphyry's book *On the Predicables* into Latin (cf. Boethius, *First Dialogue on Porphyry*) and wrote a commentary on Cicero's *Rhetorica* and *Topica* (cf. Boethius, *Commentary on Cicero's Topica*; and the edition of Cicero's works by Orelli, where Victorinus's commentary on the *Rhetorica* is found). Although the definition of *use* discussed here is not explicitly found in the aforementioned works of Victorinus, it does seem possible to gather it from the words of his cited above (objection 1 *ad opp.*) together with this definition of *exercise*, which he sets out in his *Commentary on Cicero's Rhetorica* I, ch. 2: "Exercise is the continuation of an undertaken work." Cf. also *ibid.* ch. 25, where the definition of *habit* is discussed and *use* or *exercise* is set down [as a constituent of it].

apparatus.la: *Perturbatam lectionem Vat.* et *pro* scilicet *emendavimus ope mss. et sex primarum edd. Vide etiam supra fundam. 3, sicuti et de sequenti definitione ab Augustino data cfr. fundam. 2.*
apparatus.en: We have corrected the disturbed reading *et* of the Vatican edition (in place of *scilicet*) by means of the manuscripts and the first six editions. See also above, fundamentum 3; likewise, on the following definition given by Augustine, cf. fundamentum 2.

apparatus.la: *Vide hic lit. Magistri c. 3. in princ. — In fine propositionis Vat. male et contra mss. et ed. 1* relative *pro* relatae.
apparatus.en: See here the *littera* of the Master, ch. 3, at the beginning. — At the end of the proposition the Vatican edition wrongly, and against the manuscripts and ed. 1, reads *relative* in place of *relatae*.

apparatus.la: *Vide supra in lit. Magistri c. 2, in quo textu codd. AFGHIKSXY etc. sibi non constantes habent* venit *pro* venerit.
apparatus.en: See above in the *littera* of the Master, ch. 2, in which text the codices AFGHIKSXY etc., not consistent with one another, read *venit* in place of *venerit*.

apparatus.la: *Codd. SYZ satis bene* sit. *Mox Vat., reluctantibus mss. et edd. 1, 2, 3, post* quod *addit* duobus primis modis est actus omnis potentiae, tribus vero ultimis est actus ipsius voluntatis; *sed superflue, quia verbis immediate sequentibus idem dicitur. Dein multi codd. ut CFKLMORSUVWXYZ etc. cum edd. 2 et 3 post* communissime, *omissis verbis* et communiter, *transponunt ea post* Augustinus *simulque omittunt* et propriissime, *sic legendo:* Communiter vero et proprie actus est ipsius voluntatis; *quae lectio praecedentibus manifeste contradicit. Codd. DPQT post* propriissime *addunt* loquendo, *id est tribus ultimis modis.*
apparatus.en: Codices SYZ have, well enough, *sit*. Next, against the manuscripts and editions 1, 2, and 3, the Vatican adds after *quod* the words *"in the first two ways it is the act of every faculty, but in the last three ways it is the act of the will itself"* — but superfluously, since the same is said in the words that immediately follow. Thereafter many codices (such as CFKLMORSUVWXYZ etc.) along with editions 2 and 3, after *communissime*, omit the words *et communiter*, transpose them after *Augustinus*, and at the same time omit *et propriissime*, reading thus: *"But commonly and properly the act is of the will itself"* — a reading which manifestly contradicts what precedes. Codices DPQT after *propriissime* add *loquendo* — that is, [speaking] of the last three ways.

apparatus.la: *Supple cum cod. bb* uti; *Vat. autem praeter fidem mss. et ed. 1 hic addit* uti communissime sumtum, *qua additione non quidem falsus, sed alius sensus obtinetur; in lectione siquidem mss. a S. Doctore hic non datur explicita responsio ad primo obiectum, sed breviter repetitur ipsa obiectio; e contra est in lectione Vat.*
apparatus.en: Supply, with cod. bb, *uti*; the Vatican edition, however, contrary to the manuscripts and ed. 1, here adds *uti communissime sumtum* — by which addition the sense is not made false, but is rather a different one. For on the reading of the manuscripts the Holy Doctor here gives no explicit reply to the first objection, but only briefly repeats the objection itself; the reverse is the case on the Vatican reading.

apparatus.la: *Postulante maiore parte codd. FGHIRST etc. et ed. 1, posuimus modum passivum pro activo* Augustinus dicit.
apparatus.en: Following the larger group of codices (FGHIRST etc.) and ed. 1, we have set the passive form in place of the active *Augustinus dicit*.

apparatus.la: *Cod. D* secundum.
apparatus.en: Cod. D reads *secundum*.

apparatus.la: *Vat. cum recentiore cod. cc addit* quo vel, *quod tamen abest ab antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1.*
apparatus.en: The Vatican, with the more recent cod. cc, adds *quo vel*, which is nevertheless missing from the older manuscripts and ed. 1.

apparatus.la: *Ed. 1 hic et paulo infra* illud *loco* quod dicit.
apparatus.en: Ed. 1 here and a little below reads *illud* in place of *quod dicit*.

questions.titleLa: Utrum omni creato utendum sit
questions.titleEn: Whether every created thing is to be used
questions.latin:
<!-- page 32 -->

**QUAESTIO II.** *Utrum omni creato utendum sit.*

Secundo, viso quid sit *uti* per essentiam, quaeritur de *utibili*, utrum scilicet omni creato sit utendum. Et quod sic, videtur hoc modo.

1. Proverbiorum decimo sexto[^1]: «Universum propter semetipsum operatus est Deus»; ergo omnia ordinabilia sunt in Deum; sed omne ordinabile in Deum contingit ordinare; sed ordinando in Deum ordinabile recte utimur eo: ergo omni creato contingit uti; ergo omnibus est utendum.

2. Item, ens et bonum convertuntur[^2]; sed omne bonum creatum est diligendum; sed ex diligendo est *uti*, cum semper sit ad finem: ergo omni creato est utendum.

3. Item, omni virtute contingit recte uti: ergo et e contrario vitiis malisque uti contingit, sicut aliqua virtus respicit mala poenae, ut patientia, et aliqua mala culpae, ut poenitentia; ergo contingit recte uti malis, sive poenae sive culpae: ergo etc.

4. Item, «Opposita nata sunt fieri circa idem»[^3]; sed contingit recte uti bonis creatis: ergo et malis creatis: ergo omnibus est utendum.

**Sed contra.**

1. Caritas est per quam recte utimur et diligimus; sed, sicut dicit Augustinus in *Doctrina christiana*[^4]: «Tantum quatuor diligenda sunt ex caritate, scilicet Deus, nos ipsi, proximus et corpus nostrum»; ergo tantum illa quatuor sunt diligenda, quorum tria sunt creata; ergo non omni creato est utendum.

2. Item, non omne quod subest voluntati subest dominio voluntatis quantum ad usum — ut patet de rebus naturae necessariis et huiusmodi —: ergo non omne creatum est utibile.

3. Item, Augustinus in libro de *Doctrina christiana*[^5]: «Aliqua nullo bono fine possunt fieri», ut peccata; sed quibus nullo bono fine utendum est, illis non est utendum: ergo non omnibus est utendum.

4. Item, omni malo semper abutimur, quia nullus est ipsius usus bonus; sed abusio non est usus: ergo non omni creato, quod est malum, contingit recte uti: ergo non omnibus est utendum.

**Conclusio.**

*Non omni ex creato possumus uti ut instrumento, neque ut habitu, neque ut actu medio; omnibus tamen ex iis possumus uti ut obiecto, quod approbandum vel respuendum est, vel approbando, vel acceptando, vel tolerando, vel respuendo.*

**Respondeo.** Dicendum, quod *aliquo uti* dicitur quatuor modis: aut sicut instrumento, quo mediante operamur; aut sicut habitu, quo informamur; aut sicut actu medio, quo ad ultimum tendimus, ut est habitus fidei, quo tendimus in ultimum; aut sicut obiecto, ad quod inclinamur; et sic omnibus contingit uti et abuti. Omnia enim possunt sumi in facultatem voluntatis ad approbandum vel respuendum; et hoc patet per Augustinum libro octoginta trium *Quaestionum*[^6]: «Utimur assumendis vel respuendis ad valetudinem, tolerandis ad patientiam, ordinandis ad iustitiam».

Item, Augustinus decimo *de Trinitate*[^7]: «Voluntas totam intelligentiam capit, dum utor omni eo quod intelligo»; sed mala intelliguntur: ergo contingit uti malis.

<!-- page 33 -->

Aliter tamen utimur bonis, aliter malis. Ratio enim ordinationis in bonis non tantum est ex parte ordinantis, sed etiam ex parte ordinati, quia per se bona sunt utibilia et ordinabilia, et de sui natura; sed in malis ratio ordinationis non est ex parte ordinatorum, sed potius ex parte ordinantis; et ideo mala non dicuntur utibilia.

Unde nota, quod, cum *uti* sit assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis, hoc potest esse quadrupliciter: vel in facultatem voluntatis operantis[^8], sicut est de his quae proprie pertinent ad usum humanum; vel in facultatem voluntatis acceptantis, sicut est dilectio proximi et huiusmodi; vel in facultatem voluntatis tolerantis, sicut sunt mala poenae; vel in facultatem voluntatis respuentis, et sic assumuntur mala culpae et ordinantur. Primis duobus modis intelligitur illud: «Cuius usus bonus etc.».

**Ad 1.** Ad illud ergo quod obiicitur de caritate, quod tantum tria creata sunt diligenda: dicendum, quod diligi aliquid ex caritate hoc est ordinari in summum bonum, quod per se caritas diligit. Hoc autem contingit dupliciter: aut enim contingit ordinare quod natum est devenire in finem — et sic tantum tria creata diligenda sunt ex caritate —; aut illud per quod devenire est in summum bonum; et quia hoc potest esse suo modo per omnem creaturam, omnis creatura potest diligi ex caritate, et omni creatura contingit uti.

**Ad 2.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod non omnia subiacent voluntati: dicendum, quod aliquid dicitur subesse dominio voluntatis dupliciter: aut quantum ad esse ipsius rei, et sic non omnia subiacent; aut quantum ad actum voluntatis, qui est in respuendo ipsam rem vel approbando, et hoc propter se vel propter aliud; et tali modo omnia subiacent voluntati nostrae, scilicet quantum ad actum appetitionis vel respuitionis, licet non primo modo.

**Ad 3–4.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod quaedam nullo bono fine possunt fieri, similiter, quod semper vitiis abutimur: dicendum, quod obiicitur secundum viam qua contingit uti aliquo ut actu medio, et sic non contingit uti peccato; vel sicut habitu regulante, similiter; contingit tamen eo uti sicut obiecto recte per motum contritionis et detestationis.
questions.english:
<!-- page 32 -->

**Question 2.** *Whether every created thing is to be used.*

In the second place, having seen what *use* is in essence, the question is asked concerning the *usable*, namely whether every created thing is to be used. That it is, seems to follow in this way.

1. Proverbs 16[^1]: "The Lord has made all things for his own sake"; therefore all things are orderable toward God; but whatever is orderable toward God can be ordered; and in ordering the orderable toward God, we rightly use it: therefore every created thing admits of use; therefore every created thing is to be used.

2. Again, being and good are convertible[^2]; but every created good is to be loved; and to love something is to use it, since love always tends toward an end: therefore every created thing is to be used.

3. Again, we can rightly use every virtue: therefore, conversely, we can also use vices and evils — as some virtue bears upon the evils of punishment (as patience does) and another bears upon the evils of guilt (as repentance does); therefore we can rightly use evils, whether of punishment or of guilt: therefore etc.

4. Again, "Opposites are by nature concerned with the same thing"[^3]; but we can rightly use created goods: therefore we can rightly use created evils as well: therefore every created thing is to be used.

**On the contrary.**

1. Charity is that by which we rightly use and love; but, as Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*[^4]: "Only four things are to be loved out of charity — namely, God, ourselves, our neighbor, and our own body"; therefore only those four are to be loved and referred to the end; and of these, only three are created: therefore not every created thing is to be used.

2. Again, not everything that is subject to the will is subject to the will's dominion with respect to use — as is clear in the case of the necessities of nature and the like: therefore not every created thing is usable.

3. Again, Augustine in *On Christian Doctrine*[^5]: "Some things can be done for no good end" — such as sins; but what cannot be done for a good end cannot be used [for a good end]: therefore not every created thing is to be used.

4. Again, we always *misuse* any evil, since it has no good use at all; but misuse is not use: therefore a created evil cannot be rightly used: therefore not every created thing is to be used.

**Conclusion.**

*Not every created thing can we use as an instrument, nor as a habit, nor as an act in the middle [of willing]; but every created thing we can use as an object — an object to be either approved or refused, by approving, by accepting, by enduring, or by refusing.*

**Reply.** I answer that *to use something* is said in four ways: either as an instrument, by whose mediation we act; or as a habit, by which we are informed; or as an act in the middle, by which we advance toward the end (as the habit of faith is that by which we tend toward our ultimate end); or as an object, toward which we are inclined. In this last sense, everything admits of both use and misuse, for all things can be taken up into the power of the will either for approval or for refusal. And this is clear from Augustine in the *Book of Eighty-Three Questions*[^6]: "We use things to be taken up or refused for health, things to be endured for patience, things to be ordered for justice."

Again, Augustine in Book X *On the Trinity*[^7]: "The will takes up the whole intelligence, while I use everything I understand"; but evils are understood: therefore we can use evils.

<!-- page 33 -->

We use goods in one way, however, and evils in another. For the reason of ordering in the case of goods lies not only on the side of the orderer but also on the side of what is ordered, since good things are by their own nature usable and orderable; whereas in the case of evils the reason of ordering does not lie on the side of the things ordered but rather on the side of the orderer — and this is why evils are not called *usable*.

Note, then, that since *to use* is to take something into the power of the will, this can happen in four ways: either into the power of the *operating* will[^8], as with the things that properly pertain to human use; or into the power of the *accepting* will, as with love of neighbor and the like; or into the power of the *enduring* will, as with the evils of punishment; or into the power of the *refusing* will — and so the evils of guilt are taken up and ordered. The first two ways are meant in the [Philosopher's] dictum: "That whose use is good, etc."

**Reply to 1.** To the objection from charity — that only three created things are to be loved —: it must be said that to love something out of charity is to refer it to the highest good, which charity itself loves for its own sake. This can happen in two ways: either by ordering that which is of itself fitted to reach the end — and in this way only three created things are to be loved out of charity —; or by ordering that *through* which one reaches the highest good. And since this latter can happen in its own way through every creature, every creature can be loved out of charity, and every creature admits of use.

**Reply to 2.** To the objection that not all things are subject to the will: it must be said that something is said to be subject to the dominion of the will in two ways: either with respect to the very being of the thing — and in this way not all things are subject —; or with respect to the act of the will, which consists in refusing or approving a thing (and this either for its own sake or for something else) — and in this way all things are subject to our will, namely with respect to the act of desiring or refusing, even though not in the former way.

**Reply to 3–4.** To the objections that some things can be done for no good end, and that we always misuse vices: it must be said that the objection is raised in terms of the way in which we can use something as an act in the middle — and in this way we cannot use sin; or as a regulating habit — similarly so. But we can still use it *as an object* rightly, through the act of contrition and detestation.

I. Hanc et sequentem quaestionem antiqui doctores sub una quaestione et minus accurate tractare solent. — Ostensum iam supra est, quod *uti* in sensu activo sit solius voluntatis; in secunda hac quaestione inquiritur, ad quae obiecta se extendat usus voluntatis, sive quibus rebus uti passive conveniat. In responsione S. Doctor primo ponit quadruplicem distinctionem circa obiecta voluntatis ordinanda et resolvit quaestionem in genere. Quoad primum membrum huius distinctionis, patet quod voluntas non possit omnia assumere in facultatem suam ut iis utatur sicut instrumento. Nam aliquae potentiae ipsius animae non subiacent imperio voluntatis; unde vocantur pure naturales, ut potentiae vegetativae. Secundo, incidendo in specialem quaestionem, scilicet quo sensu quis malis uti possit, iterum quadrupliciter distinguit modum voluntatis ordinantis, scilicet operantis, acceptantis, tolerantis et respuentis. Hic usus mali ex parte ordinantis est «usus per accidens», ut bene dicit Richardus (hic q. 2 ad ult.), «eo quod ordinatum aliunde accipit ordinabilitatem, scilicet a voluntate». — Circa hanc quaestionem de usu mali S. Thom. (hic loc. cit.) aliis verbis quam S. Bonaventura loquitur, sed in sententia nulla est differentia, immo in S. II. II. q. 78, a. 4. Angelicus etiam in modo loquendi cum illo convenit.

II. Alex. Hal., S. p. III, q. 61, m. 1. — Scot., hic q. 3 et 5, et *Quodl.* q. 17. — S. Thom., hic q. 2, a. 3; S. I. II. q. 16, a. 3. — B. Albert. questions.englishScholion:
**I.** The older doctors are accustomed to treat this and the following question together as a single question, and less accurately. — We have already shown above that *use* in its active sense belongs to the will alone; in this second question Bonaventure asks to which objects the use of the will extends, or to what things it is fitting that use be applied *passively*. In his reply the holy Doctor first sets down a fourfold distinction regarding the objects to be ordered by the will, and resolves the question in a general way. As for the first member of the distinction, it is clear that the will cannot take all things into its power so as to use them as an instrument. For certain powers of the soul itself are not subject to the command of the will — and hence are called *purely natural*, like the vegetative powers. Second, turning to the special question of the sense in which one can use evils, he again distinguishes the will's mode of ordering in four ways: as operating, as accepting, as enduring, and as refusing. This use of evil on the side of the one ordering is a "use by accident," as Richard [of Mediavilla] rightly says (here q. 2 *ad ult.*): "for what is ordered receives its orderability from elsewhere — namely from the will." — On this question concerning the use of evil, Thomas (*loc. cit.*) speaks in different words from Bonaventure, but there is no difference in the substance; indeed in *Summa theologiae* II–II, q. 78, a. 4, the Angelic Doctor even agrees with him in manner of expression.

**II.** Alexander of Hales, *Summa* III, q. 61, m. 1. — Scotus, here q. 3 and 5, and *Quodlibet* q. 17. — Thomas Aquinas, here q. 2, a. 3; *Summa theologiae* I–II, q. 16, a. 3. — Albert the Great, here aa. 10–11. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 1, a. 2 — who follows Bonaventure so closely that Dionysius the Carthusian says of him: "Peter, who wrote after Bonaventure, seems to have taken his own reply from Bonaventure himself." — Richard of Mediavilla, here a. 1, q. 2. — Giles of Rome, here 2nd principium, q. 3. — Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 72, q. 3, n. 11. — Durandus, here q. 4. — Dionysius the Carthusian, here q. 2. — Biel, here q. 1.

---

questions.notes:
- **Chunk scope.** This chunk covers Q. II in its entirety on printed pp. 32–33: the four *videtur quod* arguments on p. 32 (below the scholion for Q. I), the four *sed contra* arguments, the *conclusio*, the *respondeo* (which bridges pp. 32–33), the four *ad*-replies, and the two-part scholion that closes Q. II on p. 33 (before the Q. III header).

- **Title correction vs. PLAN.md.** The PLAN.md guessed *"Utrum contingat uti malis"* as the title of this question. The actual printed title on p. 32 is **"Utrum omni creato utendum sit"** ("Whether every created thing is to be used"). The question about *using evils* is one strand *within* this question, not its framing — Bonaventure takes it up because arguments 3–4 and the *ad*-replies 3–4 raise it.

- **Chunking correction.** The legacy chunk `vol1/legacy/bon-sent-I-d1-a1-q2.md` was a triple-conflation: it began mid-sentence inside the *respondeo* of Q. II ("…quae mox nominata coniuncta sunt malo…"), then ran through all of Q. III (*Utrum solo bono creato utendum sit*, which is already in the new format as `bon-sent-I-d1-a1-q3.md`), and ran on into the start of Art. II Q. unica (*Utrum frui sit actus voluntatis*) before being cut off mid-reply. This rebuild recovers the entire first half of Q. II (printed p. 32 — the fundamenta, sed contra, conclusio, and the opening of the respondeo) that the legacy chunker had silently dropped. The legacy file has been moved to `vol1/legacy/`.

- **Key terms** (per project glossary): *uti* → use; *utibile* → usable; *abuti* → misuse; *ordinare / referre* → order / refer; *facultas voluntatis* → power of the will; *operantis / acceptantis / tolerantis / respuentis* (of the will) → operating / accepting / enduring / refusing; *mala poenae / mala culpae* → evils of punishment / evils of guilt.

- **"Use by accident"** (*usus per accidens*). The scholion glosses Bonaventure's fourth mode (the will as *respuens*, refusing the evils of guilt) with Richard of Mediavilla's phrase: the evil thing receives its orderability "from elsewhere" — that is, from the ordering will itself, not from the thing's own nature. The English preserves "use by accident" as a technical phrase.

- **Vision transcription status.** This is a first-pass vision re-OCR of printed pp. 32–33 (PDF pp. 134–135). The Latin body for p. 33 was cross-checked against the legacy raw-OCR (in `vol1/legacy/bon-sent-I-d1-a1-q2.md`) and harmonized where the legacy text was more legible. A handful of apparatus readings — particularly the numbered references — should be verified on a second vision pass at higher image resolution before publication. The Quaracchi sigla list for Vol I (vol. I prolegomena) has not yet been populated in `apparatus-sigla.json`, so variant readings against specific codices are recorded verbatim rather than tooltip-expanded.

questions.titleLa: Utrum solo bono creato utendum sit
questions.titleEn: Whether only a created good is to be used
questions.latin:
<!-- page 34 -->

**QUAESTIO III.** *Utrum solo bono creato utendum sit.*

Tertio, ostenso utrum omni creato sit utendum et[^1] omni alio a Deo, est quaestio, utrum solo bono creato sit utendum. Et quod sic, videtur.

1. «Omne bonum aut est finis, aut ad finem»[^2]; sed solo bono, quod est ad finem, est utendum, quia ratio utilis est ducere in finem: ergo cum solum bonum creatum sit ad finem, solo bono creato est utendum.

2. Item, omne bonum aut est creatum, aut increatum. Sed si contingit uti bono increato, contingit illud referre ad aliud: aut ergo ad creatum, aut[^3] increatum; sed non ad increatum, quia non est nisi unum increatum: ergo ad creatum. Sed sic refertur terminus ad viam et causa ad effectum; sed hoc est abusio, non usus: ergo solo bono creato sive creatura est utendum.

3. Item, Augustinus in libro *Octoginta trium Quaestionum*[^4] dividit *honestum* contra *utile*: ergo nullum utile honestum vel e converso; sed Deus est honestum per essentiam: ergo Deo non est utendum.

4. Item, videtur quod non solum non sit utendum Deo sive bono increato, sed uti eo semper sit peccatum mortale, quia Augustinus in libro *Octoginta trium Quaestionum*[^5] dicit: «Summa perversitas est frui utendis et uti fruendis»; sed qui utitur bono increato, utitur bono fruendo: ergo etc.

**Sed contra.**

1. Contingit Deo recte servire intuitu mercedis, quia multi sunt boni mercenarii, ut dicit Ambrosius[^6]; sed non contingit Deo servire nisi amando: ergo contingit Deum recte amare intuitu mercedis; sed sic amans utitur Deo, quia refert ad aliud: ergo etc.

2. Item, sic summa bonitas habet se ad amorem, sicut[^7] summa veritas ad cognitionem; sed contingit veritatem creatam cognoscere clarius sine praeiudicio summae veritatis et sine errore: ergo similiter contingit aliam bonitatem quam summam ardentius diligere sine praeiudicio summae bonitatis et deordinatione: ergo contingit amore ordinato aliud plus diligi quam Deum: ergo contingit Deum diligi propter aliud ordinate et ita uti eo.

3. Item, videtur quod nullum peccatum sit, cum quis utitur Deo propter suam salutem, quia «cuius finis bonus, ipsum bonum»[^8]; sed huius usus bonus est, scilicet nostra salus: ergo usus Dei bonus: ergo non erit peccatum.

4. Item, usus Dei aut est bonus; et sic utendum Deo; aut est malus; et sic Deus malus, quia «cuius usus malus, ipsum malum»[^9]; quod si Deus bonus, et eius usus bonus: ergo Deo est utendum.

**Conclusio.**

*Solo bono creato est utendum, et bono increato uti est abuti.*

**Respondeo.** Dicendum, quod solo bono creato est utendum, quia, si bono increato utimur, semper est abusus, et abusus talis est mortale peccatum propter perversitatem in finem[^10] cum delectatione, et propter voluntatis inordinationem, quae minus diligit ipsum *quo* utitur, quam *propter quod* utitur.

<!-- page 35 -->

**Ad 1.** Ad illud ergo quod obiicitur, quod contingit recte servire Deo intuitu mercedis; dicendum, quod illa merces aut est ipse Deus, sicut dixit Abrahae Genesis decimo quinto[^11]: «*Ego merces tua*»; et sic intuens mercedem non utitur, quia non refert ad aliud; aut merces illa est aliud, et tunc potest eam quis intueri aut ut causam moventem; et sic est malus mercenarius[^12]; aut ut rationem inducentem; et sic bonus, et hoc modo non utitur.

**Ad 2.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod clarior cognitio creaturae non praeiudicat Creatori, ergo etc.; dicendum, quod non est simile, quia claritas cognitionis non est in nostra potestate, sed ardor affectionis est in nostra potestate; ideo requiritur a nobis, quod istum ordinemus, non illam[^13]. Aliquis tamen actus cognitionis est in nostra potestate, utpote actus fidei, quo si aliquis assentiat veritati primae propter aliud, bene praeiudicat veritati, sicut amare propter aliud, bonitati.

**Ad 3.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod finis usus Dei est bonus; dicendum, quod finis dicitur bonus dupliciter: aut quantum ad substantiam, aut quantum ad intentionem finiendi; et propositio illa intelligitur quantum ad intentionem finiendi, et haec[^14] consistit in recta ordinatione.

**Ad 4.** Ad ultimum dicendum, quod illa propositio[^15] intelligitur de habentibus ordinationem ad finem, sed non de ipso fine. — Vel intelligitur de actu naturali ipsarum rerum et proprio, qui frequentius ab ipsa re elicitur, non de ordinatione in[^16] finem; et sic non valet propositio ad propositum.
questions.english:
<!-- page 34 -->

**Question 3.** *Whether only a created good is to be used.*

Third, having shown whether everything created is to be used, and[^1] everything other than God, the question arises whether only a created good is to be used. And that it is, seems to follow thus.

1. "Every good is either an end or [is ordered] to an end"[^2]; but only a good that is [ordered] to an end is to be used, since the meaning of *useful* is to lead toward an end: therefore, since only a created good is [ordered] to an end, only a created good is to be used.

2. Again, every good is either created or uncreated. But if one can use the uncreated good, then one can refer it to something else: either to something created or[^3] to something uncreated; but not to something uncreated, since there is only one uncreated [being]: therefore to something created. But in that case a terminus is referred to the way and a cause to its effect; and this is misuse, not use: therefore only a created good — that is, a creature — is to be used.

3. Again, Augustine in the book *On Eighty-Three Questions*[^4] divides *the honorable* (*honestum*) against *the useful* (*utile*): therefore nothing useful is honorable, or conversely; but God is honorable by essence: therefore God is not to be used.

4. Again, it seems that not only is God, or the uncreated good, not to be used, but that to use him is always mortal sin — for Augustine in the book *On Eighty-Three Questions*[^5] says: "The greatest perversity is to enjoy things that are to be used and to use things that are to be enjoyed"; but he who uses the uncreated good uses a good that is to be enjoyed: therefore etc.

**On the contrary.**

1. One may rightly serve God with an eye to reward, for there are many good hirelings, as Ambrose says[^6]; but one cannot serve God except by loving [him]: therefore one may rightly love God with an eye to reward; but one who so loves uses God, since he refers him to something else: therefore etc.

2. Again, the highest goodness stands to love as[^7] the highest truth stands to knowledge; but one can know a created truth more clearly without prejudice to the highest truth and without error: therefore, likewise, one can love some goodness other than the highest more ardently without prejudice to the highest goodness and without disorder: therefore one can by an ordered love love something more than God: therefore one can love God for the sake of something else in an ordered way, and thus use him.

3. Again, it seems there is no sin when someone uses God for the sake of his own salvation, because "whose end is good, the thing itself is good"[^8]; but the end of this use is good, namely our salvation: therefore the use of God is good: therefore there will be no sin.

4. Again, the use of God is either good — and so God is to be used — or it is evil, and so God is evil, because "whose use is evil, the thing itself is evil"[^9]; and if God is good, then his use is also good: therefore God is to be used.

**Conclusion.**

*Only a created good is to be used, and to use the uncreated good is to misuse it.*

**Reply.** I answer that only a created good is to be used, because, if we use the uncreated good, it is always misuse, and such misuse is mortal sin, on account of the perversity [of turning] into an end[^10] with delight, and on account of the will's disorder, which loves that *by which* it uses less than that *on account of which* it uses.

<!-- page 35 -->

**Reply to 1.** To the objection that one may rightly serve God with an eye to reward, it must be said that that reward is either God himself — as was said to Abraham in Genesis 15[^11]: "*I am thy reward*" — and in that case one who looks to the reward does not use, since he does not refer it to anything else; or that reward is something else, and then one can look to it either as a moving cause — and so one is a bad hireling[^12] — or as a prompting reason; and in that way one is good, and in this way one does not use [God].

**Reply to 2.** To the objection that a clearer knowledge of the creature does not prejudice the Creator, therefore etc., it must be said that the two cases are not parallel, because clarity of knowledge is not in our power, but the ardor of affection is in our power; therefore it is required of us that we order the latter, not the former[^13]. Yet some act of knowledge is in our power — namely, the act of faith — by which, if someone assents to the first truth for the sake of something else, he does indeed prejudice the [first] truth, just as to love [something] for the sake of something else [prejudices] goodness.

**Reply to 3.** To the objection that the end of the use of God is good, it must be said that an end is called good in two ways: either with respect to its substance, or with respect to the intention of bringing [something] to an end (*finiendi*); and that proposition is understood with respect to the intention of bringing to an end, and this[^14] consists in right ordering.

**Reply to 4.** To the last objection, it must be said that that proposition[^15] is understood of things that have an ordering toward an end, but not of the end itself. — Or it is understood of the natural and proper act of the things themselves, which is most frequently drawn forth from the thing itself, not of [their] being ordered toward[^16] an end; and in that way the proposition does not hold for the case at hand.
questions.latinScholion:
I. In conclusione S. Doctor propositionem, quod bono increato uti sit abusus et peccatum, duplici ratione probat, quae sumitur tum ex parte finis ultimi, tum ex parte voluntatis. Ex parte finis ultimi est abusus, quia aversio a fine non fit sine contemptu eius et offensa Dei, uti probatur II *Sent.* d. 42, a. 2, q. 1, et a. 3, q. 2; ex parte voluntatis propter inordinationem, quia voluntas, quando Deo utitur, in aliquo creato ponit finem; sed finis est melior his quae sunt ad finem (infra d. 29, a. 1, q. 1 in corp.) et «quantum est de se, dicit excessum bonitatis respectu eius, quod est ad finem» (ibid. ad 4). Ex quo patet inordinatio in proposito. Voluntas enim in utendo minus diligit medium quam finem. Ad rem facit illud generalissimum principium Aristotelis, toties a S. Doctore repetitum: *Propter quod unumquodque (tale) est, illud magis est*. Cfr. etiam hic dub. 6, ubi dicit, quod omnis res sit aut finis, aut medium ad finem, aut perveniens ad finem. — Quoad solut. ad 1, nempe quomodo Deo servire possimus intuitu mercedis, cfr. II *Sent.* d. 38, a. 1, q. 3 ad 2 et III *Sent.* d. 27, a. 2, q. 2. — Quoad axioma *Cuius finis bonus, ipsum quoque bonum* (ad 3), cfr. II *Sent.* d. 38, a. 1, q. 1.

II. Quoad ipsam quaestionem: Alex. Hal., *Summa*, p. III, q. 60, m. 3, a. 1 et 2, et p. II, q. 142, m. 2. — Ceteros auctores videsis in Scholio ad praecedentem quaestionem.
